body.objective: Students will be able to compare work to industry standards.
body.iCan: I can compare work to industry standards.
successCriteria: I can compare my work to industry standards and benchmarks
I can document projects with photos, process and reflection
I can assemble a professional portfolio
body.hook: When you apply to a culinary program, a design school or an apprenticeship, they want proof you can do the work to industry standards. A portfolio of documented projects is that proof.

vocabulary.definition: The level of quality expected by professionals in a field.
An example of excellent work used for comparison.
Systems that make sure work meets standards consistently.
Photos, notes and records showing how work was done.
A curated collection of your best work as evidence of skill.
Thinking critically about what worked and what you'd change.

study.title: Prove It
study.question: How do professionals show their work meets industry standards?
study.passage:
Part 1, Benchmarks (15 minutes): Find two professional examples in your CTS area (a published recipe photo, a cabinetmaker's joint, a fashion house's finishing, a professional website). List what makes them industry quality: precision, consistency, finish, function, presentation.
Part 2, Compare (10 minutes): Place your best project beside a benchmark. Rate each quality on a 1–4 scale and identify the biggest gap.
Part 3, Document (20 minutes): For two projects, create a portfolio entry:
• Title and date
• The brief or client
• Three process photos (planning, making, finishing) plus one final photo on a clean background with good light
• Skills and tools used
• Standard met (for example "Joints flush within 0.5 mm")
• Reflection: what worked, what you'd improve, what you learned
Part 4, Assemble (10 minutes): Choose a format (digital slides, website, binder) and order: strongest project first. Add a cover page with your name, area and a two-line profile.

examples.title: Benchmark
examples.problem: What makes a professional cake photo "industry standard"?
examples.answer: Even crumb, clean slices, consistent layers, good light, uncluttered plating

examples.title: Gap
examples.problem: Your joints have 1 mm gaps; the benchmark has none. Action?
examples.answer: Use a sharper saw and dry-fit before gluing

examples.title: Documentation
examples.answer: It proves you designed it and shows your thinking

examples.title: Reflection
examples.answer: "The finish was smooth, but I'd plan more drying time; I learned patience matters as much as skill"

practice.q: Name four qualities of industry-standard work.
What should a portfolio entry include?
practice.a: Title, brief, process photos, skills, standard met, reflection.

practice.q: How should final photos be taken?
practice.a: Clean background, good light, clear focus.

practice.q: Why put your strongest project first?

practice.a: To see the gap between your work and professional quality.

practice.q: Why do post-secondary programs value process documentation?
practice.a: It shows planning, problem-solving and learning, not just a result.

practice.q: How does quality assurance differ from inspection?
practice.a: QA builds quality into the process; inspection checks results.

practice.q: How can a portfolio help in an apprenticeship interview?
practice.a: It shows real skills and work habits.

practice.q: What makes a reflection honest and useful?
practice.a: It names specific strengths, weaknesses and next steps.

misconceptions: Comparing only to classmates, not industry
Writing reflections that only praise your work
